[MTH405Abnormal Psychology Mental Health & Geriatrics](javascript:;)
2 credits
This course provides an examination of the various psychological disorders, as well as multidimensional conceptualization of mental health, clinical, and experimental perspectives of the study of psychopathology. Emphasis is placed on terminology, classification, etiology, assessment, diagnosis, and treatment of major disorders. Upon completion, students should be able to distinguish between normal and abnormal behavior patterns as well as demonstrate knowledge of etiology, symptoms, and therapeutic techniques related to music. 
[MTH410Music Therapy and Communication: Understanding Therapeutic Needs](javascript:;)
1 credits
Observation of therapeutic activities ME and role-play. 
[MTH430MTH Internship](javascript:;)
2 credits
The observation internship is oriented towards participation in communities of practice, the observation of innovative approaches and modes of intervention. 
[ Specialization - Emphasis: Sacred Music](javascript:;)
[EMS305Voice and Ear Physiology and Didactic Singing](javascript:;)
1 credits
Singing is an art and a profession. This course treats the anatomy, the physiology, the acoustics, the phonetics and the technique of the voice and the ear. 
[ETH345Field Research in Musicology and Ethnomusicology](javascript:;)
2 credits
This course is an introduction to musicological and ethnomusicological research. It includes four parts: objects and methods, sources, musical research and presentation standards. Field research in musicology and ethnomusicology is a dynamic and interdisciplinary process that combines the study of music with cultural anthropology, sociology, linguistics, and other disciplines. It allows researchers to gain a deep and holistic understanding of music in its cultural context, contribute to the preservation of musical traditions, and promote intercultural understanding. 
[MSS310History of Sacred Music I](javascript:;)
2 credits
This course is an introduction to music in its relation to religion. It includes general concepts on religion, philosophy, the sacred and their rapport with music. Subjects to study: the function of sacred music, the relationship of religion with music, tradition and renewal in sacred music; sacred music categories, forms and genres of sacred music, classification of sacred songs in the Maronite Church, and the characteristics of sacred music etc. 
[MSS311History of Sacred Music II](javascript:;)
2 credits
[MSS315Interpretation of Sacred Music (didactic)](javascript:;)
2 credits
[MSS405Gregorian Chant](javascript:;)
1 credits
Gregorian chant is the central tradition of Western plainchant, a form of monophonic, unaccompanied sacred song of the western Roman Catholic Church. Gregorian chant developed mainly in western and central Europe during the 9th and 10th centuries, with later additions and redactions. Although popular legend credits Pope St. Gregory the Great with inventing Gregorian chant, scholars believe that it arose from a later Carolingian synthesis of Roman chant and Gallican chant. Gregorian chants were organized initially into four, then eight, and finally 12 modes. Gregorian melodies are traditionally written using neumes, an early form of musical notation from which the modern four-line and five-line staff developed. Multi-voice elaborations of Gregorian chant, known as organum, were an early stage in the development of Western polyphony. Gregorian chant was traditionally sung by choirs of men and boys in churches, or by men and women of religious orders in their chapels. It is the music of the Roman Rite, performed in the Mass and the monastic Office. Although Gregorian chant supplanted or marginalized the other indigenous plainchant traditions of the Christian West to become the official music of the Christian liturgy, Ambrosian chant still continues in use in Milan, and there are musicologists exploring both that and the Mozarabic chant of Christian Spain. Although Gregorian chant is no longer obligatory, the Roman Catholic Church still officially considers it the music most suitable for worship. During the 20th century, Gregorian chant underwent a musicological and popular resurgence. 
[MSS415Syro-Maronite Chant I](javascript:;)
1 credits
The Christian churches of the East are the guardians of a tradition dating back to the early days of Christianity. The Syriac Church is part of a community of independent Christian churches that were born in the East as a result of the separation from the Church of the West. The Syriac church music is vocal, and its liturgical language is Syriac. Ancient language, it is a late dialect of Aramaic (the language spoken by Christ). Syriac is still spoken today, both within the Church and outside. The Syriac scholars who exerted a lasting influence on the Christian world, include St-Ephrem (306-373), Jacob of Serugh (451-521), St. Severus, Patriarch of Antioch (died 538), Jacob of Edessa (died 708) and Bar Hebraeus (died in 1286). Saint Ephraim has composed a very large number of hymns and liturgies. As is the case in all the churches of the East, the Sunday mass dominates the spiritual and religious life of the faithful. It is celebrated by the priest who stands at the altar while the deacons, placed in two groups or more exactly in two choirs on each side of the altar, sing alternately (antiphonal) all by assisting the priest in the celebration of the mass. Syriac chant places its melodic styles (qinto) within an overall unit (oktōēchos, or set of eight modes). The texts of the sacred songs were compiled in more than twenty liturgical books that include a comprehensive collection of hymns. The texts of the prayers are contained in fifteen liturgical books, including the shkhimo or book of offices for the days of the week, the book of the Holy Mass, the fanqith, or book of prayers for the year (Sundays, holy days...) and the book betkaz (treasure of melodies), complete collection of Church songs. 
[MSS416Syro-Maronite Chant II](javascript:;)
1 credits
The Syro-Maronite chant repertoire includes hymns, psalms, and various liturgical texts, which are sung during different parts of the Maronite Mass and the divine office. This course consists in the study and analysis of different chants and different forms, the text, the modality, the notation, the composition, etc.The Syro-Maronite chant reflects the deep historical and theological roots of the Maronite community and continues to be an essential element of their religious expression. 
[MSS420Byzantine Chant I](javascript:;)
1 credits
The Aim of this course is to go through the foundations of Byzantine chant and its three ‘genera’: the diatonic, the chromatic, and the enharmonic; its eight ‘modes’ or ‘tones’; its roots: Greek (as proven by historians who suggest that as Christianity “took over the language of the Greeks… so also it took over the religious music of the Greeks and adapted it to its own needs”) Non-Greek ( as proven by historians who tend to assert, “the basis of the Christian music during the early centuries was not simply Greek, but Graeco-Roman” and Hebrew); and its key characteristics: as being Entirely vocal, no use of instruments, Monophonic, using only melodies in one part, Antiphonic, executed by two alternately chanting choirs, ison, the holding-note, and leading the chant. As well as the difference between Orthodox Byzantine chants and Catholic Byzantine Chants. 
[MSS421Byzantine Chant II](javascript:;)
1 credits
This course studies some key of Byzantine chant like the liturgical use, system of notation system, modality, melismatic, responsorial singing, etc. and the liturgical roles. 
[MSS425Quranic Chant](javascript:;)
1 credits
[MSS430Armenian Chant](javascript:;)
1 credits
This course Covers the Armenian chant, composed in one of eight modes, written in khaz, a form of indigenous musical notation. As well as many the ancient origin of these chants, extending to pre-Christian times, while others are relatively modern, including several composed by Saint Mesrop Mashtots, who re-introduced the Armenian alphabet. Some of the best performers of these chants or sharakans, are at the Holy Cathedral of Etchmiadzin, and include the late soprano Lusine Zakaryan. The Armenian religious music that remained liturgical until Komitas Vardapet introduced polyphony in the end of the 19th century. Apart from his contribution to religious music, Komitas may be considered the founder of modern classical Armenian music. From 1899 to 1910, he travelled through the Armenian highlands and collected more than 3,000 folk tunes many of which he harmonized and transformed into Lieder. 
[MSS435World Sacred Music & Dances](javascript:;)
1 credits
Ceremonial music and dances are integral to cultural expressions and rituals across the world. They play a significant role in religious ceremonies, rites of passage, and traditional celebrations. Here’s a glimpse of some ceremonial music and dances from different cultures: Hula (Hawaii): Hula, Samba (Brazi), Dandiya Raas (India), Taiko Drumming (Japan), Whirling Dervishes (Turkey and Middle East), Maori Haka (New Zealand), Flamenco (Spain), Gamelan (Indonesia), Zulu War Dance (South Africa), Scottish Highland Games (Scotland), etc. These forms of expression play a vital role in preserving cultural heritage, conveying meaning, and bringing communities together during significant events and celebrations. 
[THEO355Introduction to Sacramental Theology and Liturgy](javascript:;)
3 credits
[ Specialization - Emphasis: Musicology](javascript:;)
[MUG205Musicological Research](javascript:;)
1 credits
This course is an introduction to musicological research. It includes four parts: objects and methods, sources, musicological research and presentation standards. It is essentially practical and aims to help future musicologists and researchers become apprentices in their undergraduate studies. 
[MUG330Music Languages](javascript:;)
2 credits
The goal of this course is to give to the students a general idea about the evolution of musical language from its beginning to the twentieth century: the scale of harmonics; the cycle of fifths, consonance and attraction, tolerance, habituation, equalization, the formation of the scales, relative pitch and absolute pitch, the organization of the sounds in space and in time, the melodic order and the harmonic order, the chromatic scale; the irregular and altered scales; from ditonic scale to heptatonic scale; accuracy and the acoustic systems; the equal temperament. 
[MUG335Musical Acoustics](javascript:;)
3 credits
This course concentrates on: vibratory motion of typical musical sound sources, propagation of sound, wavelength, period and frequency, pressure and acoustic intensity, the acoustic impedance speed, etc; perceived pitch, loudness and timbre of a sound; the objectively measurable properties of a sound wave; explaining how sound is generated - transformed by the musical instruments and the human voice; defining the reverberation time of a hall, using a formula relating reverberation time to the volume of the hall and the absorption of its surfaces, and discussing the acoustical properties desirable in concert halls and opera houses; microphones, amplifiers, speakers and sound captation acoustic treatment and correction. 
[MUG340Introduction to Musicology and Ethnomusicology](javascript:;)
3 credits
This course provides an introduction to concepts and approaches to music research as encountered in the co-disciplines of historical musicology and ethnomusicology. It aims to develop students’ critical thinking in areas of historiography, fieldwork, musical meaning, and aesthetics. It introduces students to some of the methodologies and research techniques employed musicology and ethnomusicology. 
[MUG410Contemporary Music](javascript:;)
3 credits
This course is open to current and transdisciplinary musical concerns. The concept for transdisciplinarity does not define a degree of specialization, but rather refers to a type of approach that allows the addressing of contemporary issues based on various disciplines and different fields of knowledge, placing the reflection beyond the mere juxtaposition of the subjects studied. The first set gives rise to learning activities that allow the student identify major issues of contemporary concern, to demonstrate the contribution of various disciplines in the understanding of a problem, through theories, concepts and methods of analysis. The second set invites the students to confront the real world and deal with a contemporary problem in a research piece where, after they have identified and analyzed the problem, they will have to justify the relevance of their proposed solutions. 
[MUG425Arab Music II](javascript:;)
3 credits
This course offers an analytical study of the older forms of music and Arabic Song: longa, Samai, Dulab, Tahmila, Bachraf, Taqsím, Mawwals, Qasîda, Taqtouqa, Mouwashah, Dawr etc. 
[THT465Performing Arts Production](javascript:;)
3 credits
Students will demonstrate knowledge of the performing arts industry, including live performance genres, production processes, careers, and work environments. They will work creatively as part of a team to prepare and execute a live performance. 
[ Specialization - Emphasis: Music Education](javascript:;)
[EDU344Computer Applications in Education](javascript:;)
3 credits
This course introduces elementary school teacher candidates to the use of computer applications in the classroom. The course covers the basics of computer hardware and software, and explores how these tools can be used to enhance teaching and learning. Students will learn to use various software applications to create multimedia content, develop lesson plans, manage student data, and facilitate communication with parents and other stakeholders. The course will also cover internet safety and ethical considerations related to the use of technology in the classroom. 
[EMU320Specialized Musical Teaching](javascript:;)
2 credits
The objectives of the course are: ­ discovering how music can be an additional means of communication for the disabled child; ­ exploring musical situations developed with children with disabilities; ­ promoting the relationship of special needs students with their environment (other children, professionals, parents etc.) by music. It deals with the issues and the values of integration today and the importance of the artistic practice of people with disabilities: access to culture, to museums etc. It also studies cases of students with different disabilities and their musical practices. A visit to institutions dealing with children with disabilities, in order to have direct observation practice, would be an integral part of this course. 
[EMU330Music Education Methods](javascript:;)
3 credits
This course provides an introduction to the best known Western music education methods: Carl Orff, Zoltan Kodály, Edgar Willems, Emile Jaques­Dalcroze, Marcel Corneloup, Maurice Chevais, Maurice Martenot, suzuki etc. 
[EMU405Music and Psychology](javascript:;)
3 credits
Music psychology is the empirical study of how humans perceive and experience music, and the resulting impact on individual, group and cultural behavior. This course will encompass an introductory exploration of music psychology across a lifespan. It explains the different stages of the musical development of the baby, child and adolescent at the sensory­motor, social/emotional, psychomotor and intellectual/communicative levels. 
[EMU410Psycho-pedagogical Approach of Musical Learning](javascript:;)
2 credits
The objective of this course is to identify methodological psychoeducational training paths for the music teachers regarding in particular the musical class learning management as it might contribute to the development of basic skills defined for music education and, more generally, social and individual student development.

2 credits

2 credits
[EMU440Scholar Musical Teaching II](javascript:;)
2 credits

2 credits

[HRG215Harmony I A](javascript:;)
1 credits
Figured Bass and given Song: A. ­ Realization of a given bass with 3 sound chords (root position, 1st and 2nd inversions). ­ Harmonization of a song given with 3 chord sounds (all positions). B. Modulations to the adjacent and distant tones, uni­tonal and modulating harmonic movements, figured bass and given song. C. Chords of the dominant 7th, with and without fundamental, regular and exceptional resolution: given bass and given song. 
[HRG225Harmony I B](javascript:;)
1 credits
[HRG315Harmony II A](javascript:;)
1 credits
Figured Bass.   
A. ­ Chords of the Dominant 9th major and minor, with and without fundamental ­ Chords of the 7th in various species.   
B. ­ Changes, delays and pedals.   
C. ­ The foreign notes: changes, delays, pedals, notes of passage, anticipation, appoggiatura, etc. 
[HRG325Harmony II B](javascript:;)
1 credits
[MUSC210Choral singing I](javascript:;)
1 credits
Choral singing closely follows the course of history. Each year the students learn to interpret, in the context of Western choral singing of the Faculty, the corresponding repertory according to the current history course. 
[MUSC215Choral Singing II](javascript:;)
1 credits
Choral singing closely follows the course of history. Each year the students learn to interpret, in the context of Western choral singing of the Faculty, the corresponding repertory according to the current history course. 
[MUSC220Music Critique and Aesthetic Judgement I](javascript:;)
1 credits
This course includes a guided reading and musical critique, taking in readings in the literature and the science of music. Each student will have to read a book (or chapters in a book) per semester and present the content to others. The criticism is about:   
- Various reports and interviews, mainly in the field of contemporary musical creation.   
- Conception, realization and animation of a series of programs devoted to classical, modern and contemporary music.   
- A roundtable around musical works by various composers.   
- A report on a festival and concerts presented as part of this festival.   
- Leaflet of a compact disc, published flyers or texts in concert programs.   
- Symposia concerning music and conferences contained therein.  

[MUSC225Music Critique and Aesthetic Judgement II](javascript:;)
1 credits
This course includes a guided reading and musical critique, taking in readings in the literature and the science of music. Each student will have to read a book (or chapters in a book) per semester and present the content to others. The criticism is about:   
- Various reports and interviews, mainly in the field of contemporary musical creation.   
- Conception, realization and animation of a series of programs devoted to classical, modern and contemporary music.   
- A roundtable around musical works by various composers.   
- A report on a festival and concerts presented as part of this festival.   
- Leaflet of a compact disc, published flyers or texts in concert programs.   
- Symposia concerning music and conferences contained therein. 
[MUSC246Arab Music I](javascript:;)
3 credits
This course aims to educate students on various aspects of Arab music, including folk and art music, theoretical and practical knowledge, the Maghreb and the Mashreq, etc. The themes to be discussed encompass a general history of Arab music, the maqams, the Arab musical scale and modal system, as well as the rhythms and musical writings of Ibn Al-Munajjim, Al-Kindi and Al-Farabi. 
[MUSC251History and Analysis of the 17th Century Music](javascript:;)
3 credits
This course will consist of an investigation of the principal styles of European music from ancient Greece to early Baroque Music. It will focus on a panoramic view of the main events, composers, genres, forms, schools, language and problems of the music during those periods. This course will also provide a deep analysis (form, genre, structure, themes, rhythm, orchestration and harmonic and polyphonic writing, language, general nature of the work...) of musical styles and composition in examples mostly selected from Greek, Medieval, Renaissance, and early Baroque Music. 
[MUSC260Introduction to Music Production and Studio Signal Flow](javascript:;)
3 credits
The course is intended for students interested in the world of sound (training, recording, publishing and editing), as well as the musical production. This is a theoretical course illustrated by examples multimedia and completed by practical application sessions. The student will be able to Interpret the specifications of mixing boards, microphones, and signal processors, explain the syntax of the audio reinforcement and recording field and discuss the implementation of sound reinforcement devices into the microphone, mixing board, amplification and speaker matrix. 
[MUSC265Organology ](javascript:;)
1 credits
The aim of the course is to introduce musical instruments, their history, their individual characteristics and their classification. The course focuses on an overview of the main currents of organology, the identification of the different families of musical instruments; it reviews the instruments mechanics, acoustics, evolution, manufacturing and their social and historical contextualization. 
[MUSC330History and Analysis of the 18th Century Music](javascript:;)
3 credits
This course opens on the baroque era, with the dawn of the classical musical style. It deals with the following subjects: French from 1661 to 1764 music, music of the Germanic countries around Bach and Handel, English music in the 18th century, the birth and diffusion of classicism in Polish music, music in Spain, the music in Italy from the death of Carissimi to the end of the eighteenth century, classicism in Austria and the German-speaking countries from the death of Telemann to the death of Beethoven, the formation of the classical style in Europe and the classical masters: Haydn and Mozart. 
[MUSC340Musical Forms](javascript:;)
3 credits
The examination of the form is a fundamental element of any analysis, because the form depends on the various components of a work, namely melody, rhythm, instrumentation, dynamics, tonal course, elements of unity and contrast ratio, relationship between text and music if it is a voice composition and other components. To understand musical forms, is to discern the sound architecture. 
[MUSC360Instrumentation](javascript:;)
1 credits
This course enhances students' knowledge of the modern orchestra while reinforcing core musicianship skills. Instrumentation study investigates the technical limitations and expressive potential of individual instruments. In examining instrumental characteristics, the unit will also cover the fundamentals of acoustics and timbre perception and will demand a thorough grasp of the harmonic series and its broader musical implications. Throughout the course, students will be required to present their own transcriptions. 
[MUSC365Lebanese Music](javascript:;)
1 credits
This course is designed to: 1 – Sensitize students to Lebanese folk music. 2 ­ Make them aware of the danger that threatens this music: a Heritage endangered. The disappearance of the songs with the disappearance of the circumstances and opportunities serving their raison d’être. The disappearance of the 'old', guardians and deliverers of the tradition. A heritage uncollected, not recorded in a scientific way. 3 – Let them discover the diversity of forms: mostly little known and unknown forms. 4 ­ Study of the poetic­musical internal structure of each form of traditional song. 
[MUSC420Choir Conducting I](javascript:;)
1 credits
This course aims to train musicians on vocals, choirs and choir conducting. It includes concepts about the human voice and its education, the choir and its training, the conductor of the choir (values, posture, technique, behavior, etc.), choral conducting (departure gesture, the fermata, the stop gestures, the syncopation and offbeat, repeat, etc). This course includes exercises on the evolution of the musical ear, on conductor gestures, on the conducting of simple meters (2/4, 3/4, 4/4).. 
[MUSC430History and Analysis of the 19th Century Music](javascript:;)
3 credits
1 - Characteristics of romantic music: themes of romanticism, individuality of style, expressive subjects, nationalism and exoticism, the use of timbers to obtain a variety of sensations and atmospheres, the use of chromatic harmony, contrasts in nuances...  
2. The vocal music, the program music, the romantic Symphony, the brief forms and developed forms.  
3. Romantic composers: Beethoven, Schubert, Schumann, Chopin, Liszt, Mendelssohn, Berlioz, Tchaikovsky, Smetana, Dvorak, Brahms, Verdi, Puccini, Wagner, Mahler. 
[SDG303Solfeggio/Dictation III](javascript:;)
2 credits
a­ Solfeggio parlati : ­ Pozzoli: appendice al primo corso from n°1 till n°31.   
b­ Solfeggio cantati: - Pozzoli: appendiceal prima corso from no1 till no27.   
c- Dictation:-Noel Gallon from no 41 till no60. - melodic intervals: all intervals, and major and minor chords. 
#### Emphasis
- Musicology (Open for Admission)  
- Music Education (Open for Admission)  
- Sacred Music (Open for Admission)  
- Music Industry (Open for Admission)  
- Music Therapy (Open for Admission)  
- Ethnomusicology (Open for Admission)  
  

#### Mission
The Faculty of Music is committed to developing confident, creative, and skilled musicians, researchers, historians of music and ethnomusicologists.  
The Faculty of Music provides opportunities for students of all majors to enhance their musical knowledge and skill, through participation in a wide variety of academic courses, performance studies, and field experiences.  
As a vital part of the University, the Faculty of Music promotes the musical arts of regional, national and international communities within the University.  

#### Program Educational Objectives
1. Graduates will be engaged in active music making and a good selection of presentations.  
2. Graduates will demonstrate desire and ability to generate innovative ideas and use effective means of communicating them.  
3. Graduates will show a mature, confident, analytical and critical approach to current activities in music and the media, which is based on an awareness and understanding of broader cultural issues.  

#### Student Learning Outcomes
a. Student will develop knowledge and skills on a major instrument or voice and the ability to sight read.  
b. Develop skills and understanding of music language and composition in a variety of styles, periods, and genres, in both Western European tradition and non­Western cultures.  
c. Develop skills of criticism and defend musical judgment, with reference to contextual meaning and aesthetic value in own work, and the work of others.  
d. Develop a comprehensive knowledge and understanding of Western musical history and its analysis, and for Arab and Lebanese music traditions.  
e. Develop technical skills and musical awareness for performance and leadership of both small and large choirs.  
f. Develop knowledge and skills in the use of technology as it applies to notating, arranging, recording, and composing music.  
g. Develop a comprehensive knowledge and understanding of musical instruments; their classification systems, and the technical aspects related to their constructions and sound qualities and their use and importance in a composition.  
h. Develop a working knowledge of music as it relates to and enhances the theater and religious experience.  
i. Develop and demonstrate understanding and appreciation of diverse non­Western and Ethnic music traditions. Specific for the Musicology Emphasis  
j. Develop research skills and the foundational background necessary to explore the social and cultural development of music from around the globe and demonstrate understanding of musical traditions and their influences.   
k. Develop an understanding of the history of sacred music and the ability to interpret various genre and styles of occidental and oriental sacred chants.  
l. Develop an understanding of child growth and development and the principles of learning, related to music.   
m. Develop the ability to teach music to a variety of age groups in a range of classroom and ensemble settings (K­12 and special learners) in an effective management of classes based on methods and materials currently utilized in music education settings.

[](javascript:;)
[](https://www.usek.edu.lb/en/international/international-affairs)[](https://outlook.office.com/book/StudentsStudyAbroadConsultancy@net.usek.edu.lb/s/cTeW5Fibx02KlNKEX3Q0wQ2?ismsaljsauthenabled)[](https://www.usek.edu.lb/erasmus-international-credits-mobility)[](https://www.usek.edu.lb/international/memberships)[](https://www.usek.edu.lb/international/international-summer-school)[](https://www.usek.edu.lb/international/study-at-usek)[](https://www.usek.edu.lb/international/incoming-mobility)[](https://www.usek.edu.lb/international/outgoing-mobility)[](https://www.usek.edu.lb/en/international/opportunities-abroad)[](https://www.usek.edu.lb/faculty/staff-mobility-2025-2026)[](https://www.usek.edu.lb/en/international/semester-abroad-opportunities)[](https://www.usek.edu.lb/usek-diplomacy-academy)[](https://www.usek.edu.lb/international/ajyal-program)[](https://www.usek.edu.lb/internationl/be-a-buddy-program)[](https://www.usek.edu.lb/international/global-engagement-certificate)[](https://www.usek.edu.lb/international/usek-nam-scholarship-program)[](https://www.usek.edu.lb/en/international/news)
##  Incoming Mobility 
Studying abroad is a life-changing experience that exposes you to new cultures, languages, and lifelong friendships. USEK offers students from partner universities the chance to join our Study Abroad program for one semester or academic year, explore campus life, and connect with local and international students.  
  

[Before your Mobility](javascript:;)
1. Get nominated by your home university  
Your home university can nominate you for a mobility at USEK, by completing and sending the Nomination Form.  
  
2. Submit your mobility application  
After receiving your nomination, the International Affairs Office (IAO) will contact you to start your mobility application process. You will need to submit the documents below before the application deadline: 
  * International Incoming Students Application Form 
  * Passport
  * Two passport-size photos
  * Official transcript
  * Copy of international health insurance

Upon your arrival at USEK, you must also submit these documents to the IAO as hard copies.  
  
3. Set your learning agreement, sign it, and send it to the IAO  
  
4. Receive your Acceptance Letter  
  
5. Apply for a visa and purchase your ticket  
Check the website of the Lebanese Embassy in your home country and start preparing the documents needed for your visa application. Make sure you have an active passport that will remain valid during your mobility period before you submit your visa application.  
Once your visa is secured, you can book your flight ticket. Please check USEK’s [Academic Calendar](https://www.usek.edu.lb/en/calendar) to make sure you arrive on campus at least one week before the beginning of the semester.  
  
6. Communicate your arrival and departure dates to the IAO
[Airport Arrival](javascript:;)
The Rafik Hariri International Airport is Lebanon’s only international airport. 
  * Entry Visa: Visa requirements depend on your nationality. To check if you are eligible for an entry visa, please visit the General Security website.
  * Transportation: Upon arrival, you can either negotiate a taxi fare at the airport or book a taxi in advance online.

  
Recommended Taxi Services: 
  * Charlie Taxi: +961 1 285 710
  * Angelo Taxi: +961 9 646 647


[Living in Lebanon](javascript:;)
**Cost of Living (Subject to change)**  
Kaslik offers a vibrant student-friendly environment with a relatively affordable cost of living compared to many European cities. In Lebanon, payments can be made in both Lebanese Pounds (LBP) and US Dollars (USD). Below is an estimated breakdown of monthly expenses: 
  * Accommodation: $400–$500/month
  * Food: $300/month
  * Leisure: $150/month

  
  
**Means of Transportation**  
1. Buses  
Buses (public and private) are an affordable and widely used mode of transport and can be hailed anywhere along the route (they do not have official stops or schedules).They operate between the north and south of the country, with the main terminus in Beirut.  
The Lebanese Commuting Company is one of the key public transport providers.  
Public buses are managed by the Railway and Public Transportation Authority.  
Always confirm the destination with the driver before boarding.  
  
2. Taxis and “Service” (pronounced “ser-vees”):  
Taxis and service are the most common transportation options.  
A service (shared taxi) is more affordable than a private taxi, but the fare must be negotiated in advance.  
Both taxis and services have red license plates and can be hailed on the street.  
When hailing a ride, specify whether you need a taxi (private ride) or a service (shared ride).  
- A taxi takes only one passenger or group and is more expensive.  
- A service takes multiple passengers along the same route, making it a budget-friendly option.  
  
**Lebanon Emergency Numbers**  
- Police: 112  
- Civil Defense: 125  
- Red Cross: 140  
- Fire Department: 175  
  
**Communication, Internet, and Wi-Fi**  
- Country Code: Lebanon’s country code is +961.  
- Mobile Providers: The two main mobile operators in Lebanon are Alfa and Touch.  
  
1. Student Mobile Plan:   
For $5 per month, You can subscribe to a student plan that includes:  
- 5 GB of data  
- 1,000 local messages  
- 180 local minutes  
  
This plan is perfect for when you are not connected to a Wi-Fi network. To get the student plan, follow the steps below:  
- For Alfa users: Purchase a Lebanese SIM card and send an SMS to 1028 with the message: “AA+ followed by your University ID” after the 20th of the month. Make sure you receive a confirmation SMS indicating your eligibility for the plan.  
- For Touch users: Download the Touch app, create an account, then go to "Touch News" and select “Student Plan” to follow the instructions after the 5th of the month.  
  
The student plan is available only for students under 25 years of age. Once you have your SIM card, please share your phone number with the Office of the Registrar at: registrar@usek.edu.lb.  
  
2. Wi-Fi Access:  
Wi-Fi is widely available in all restaurants, bars, and coffee shops. Simply ask for the Wi-Fi password when you visit.
[Be-A-Buddy Program](javascript:;)
Every international student will be paired with a USEK student volunteer, known as a Buddy, who will help them navigate student life and ease their transition. You will receive your Buddy’s contact details before your arrival. [Learn more](https://www.usek.edu.lb/internationl/be-a-buddy-program)
[Before you leave ](javascript:;)
1. Confirm your departure date with IAO  
2. Complete the feedback form  
3. Get your academic transcript  
4. Share your mobility testimonial
[Application Deadlines](javascript:;)
**May 15** for mobility in the Fall Semester.  
**October 15** for mobility in the Spring Semester.

##  Global Engagement Certificate 
The Global Engagement Certificate is available to all USEK students, offering a chance to have their global engagement officially recognized.  
  
As international skills become increasingly vital in today’s globalized world, this program encourages USEK students to actively participate in international activities and programs, helping them develop into global citizens.  
  
Students can track their global engagement through their online account and earn points based on the criteria below. To be awarded the USEK Global Engagement Certificate, students must accumulate a total of 300 points.  
  
  
Abroad |  |    
  
---|---|---  
Exchange program |  | 100 points  
Internship abroad |  | 100 points  
Short term mobility program (summer schools, study tours) |  | 100 points  
International event (conferences, competitions) |  | 50 points  
  
  
At Home  
|  |    
  
---|---|---  
Be a Buddy program |  | 75 points  
International internship/part-time work/student job at home |  | 75 points  
International/intercultural event Panelist/Speaker/Contestant  |  | 75 points  
Active participation in an international project |  | 50 points  
International/intercultural event Participant  |  | 25 points  
Second language certificate  |  | 25 points  
Third language courses |  | 50 points  
  
_Students must earn a minimum of 300 points and submit a brief report detailing their international experience in order to receive the Global Engagement Certificate._

##  AJYAL: Lebanese Heritage Education Program 
The mission of the Holy Spirit University of Kaslik (USEK) is deeply rooted in preserving and promoting Lebanese heritage across generations. USEK’s AJYAL program was developed as an authentic, yet innovative initiative that builds a profound connection to Lebanese identity, ensuring that our rich culture continues to thrive among Lebanese expatriate communities worldwide.  
  

### About AJYAL
AJYAL, or “generations” in Arabic, is a collaborative effort to strengthen cultural ties between Lebanon and its worldwide diaspora. This three-phased educational program is designed to engage Lebanese children, youth, and parents living abroad. Rooted in a dynamic and immersive learning approach, the program builds a deeper connection with Lebanese heritage, culture, and traditions. Through a blend of educational activities, cultural experiences, and community engagement, AJYAL strengthens the bond between Lebanese families and their homeland.  
  

### AJYAL’s Mission
The mission of the AJYAL program is to:  
1. preserve and promote Lebanese heritage globally by building meaningful connections across generations.  
2. encourage cross-generational dialogue to ensure that Lebanese traditions and values are passed down and celebrated.  
3. engage communities in a way that sparks curiosity, pride, and appreciation for Lebanese culture.  
4. strengthen the bond between Lebanon and its diaspora, reinforcing a shared identity.  
  

### The Program
AJYAL is structured into three phases, each tailored to different age groups and learning objectives:  
  
**Phase 1**  
The program’s first phase engages young learners through storytelling, games, and hands-on activities that introduce them to Lebanese culture, history, and traditions. Children explore the richness of Lebanon’s heritage in fun and interactive ways, creating a sense of belonging and curiosity from an early age.  
  
**Phase 2**  
AJYAL’s Phase 2 focuses on active engagement and creative exploration, encouraging teenagers and young adults to interpret and express Lebanese heritage in ways that resonate with today’s world. Building on the foundations of Phase 1, this phase moves beyond discovery and into action, where youth become storytellers, cultural contributors, and ambassadors of identity.  
Phase 2 initiatives are structured into several pillars and activities, each designed to deepen cultural understanding and strengthen community connection.  
**  
On-Campus Group**  
The AJYAL team launched the USEK on-campus AJYAL Group as part of its mission to strengthen awareness and appreciation of Lebanese heritage within the University community.  
This initiative brings together a diverse group of faculty, staff, and students who share a common interest in exploring and celebrating Lebanese cultural identity. Since its formation, the AJYAL Group has actively participated in site visits to historical and cultural landmarks across Lebanon, offering a meaningful connection to the country’s rich heritage.  
In addition to these experiences, the group hosted a vibrant on-campus event designed to engage the broader student body. The event featured a series of fun, interactive activities centered around Lebanese heritage, inviting students to take part in friendly competitions. Winners were awarded nostalgic prizes inspired by a typical Lebanese childhood, sparking a sense of cultural pride and connection to their roots.  
Through such initiatives, the AJYAL Group continues to promote cultural understanding, build community spirit, and bring Lebanese heritage to life at USEK.   
  
**Lebanese Heritage Short Film Competition 2025**  
The Holy Spirit University of Kaslik (USEK) organized the first edition of the Lebanese Heritage Short Film Competition, which is part of the AJYAL program. The awards ceremony, held under the patronage of Minister of Culture Dr. Ghassan Salameh, took place on June 12, 2025, on the University campus in Kaslik, attracting a sizeable attendance from various walks of life.   
This year’s competition, which aims to promote Lebanon’s heritage through the lens of its youth to revive the country’s national identity, attracted 64 short films by students of various Lebanese universities, spanning various majors.   
An academic committee of experts representing seven Lebanese universities, chaired by artist Georges Khabbaz and encompassing renowned film specialists, chose ten works for the final round to be evaluated based on originality, theme, directing, performance, image quality, sound, and script. Three special awards were granted based on a joint evaluation by both the selection and jury committees.  
The opening speeches were followed by a musical performance and a promotional screening of the ten finalists.  
  
Cash prizes were divided into $3,000 for first place, $2,000 for second place, and $1,000 for third place, in addition to honorary awards for Best Director (Christina Klat, ALBA), Best Theme (Amer Makki, Lebanese University), and Most Innovative Idea (Yasmin Kobeissi, USEK).  
  
The main awards were as follows: 
  * First place: Jack Mouaykel (USEK)
  * Second place: Robert Minassian (LAU)
  * Third place: Yasmin Kobeissi (USEK)

  
  
This initiative serves as an annual platform supporting Lebanese heritage preservation projects, fostering youth creativity, and highlighting art as a medium for dialogue and the construction of collective memory.  
  
**Phase 3**  
AJYAL’s Phase 3 offers sessions that help parents instill in their children a sense of pride in their Lebanese heritage, thereby ensuring intergenerational cultural continuity. Parents learn practical tools and strategies to share their cultural roots and values with younger generations, fostering a deeper sense of identity and belonging within the family.  
  
The AJYAL program has already launched in various countries, and its impact continues to expand, aiming to engage Lebanese communities worldwide, such as in the USA, Canada, UAE, KSA, Brazil, France, Australia, and South Africa.  
  

### Sustainable Development Goals
  
AJYAL aligns with USEK’s commitment to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly: 
  * SDG 4 – Quality Education
  * SDG 11 – Sustainable Cities and Communities
  * SDG 17 – Partnerships for the Goals

  
  
This unique initiative is our way to safeguard and celebrate our rich Lebanese culture. Be part of the AJYAL family, where the world becomes a classroom and Lebanese heritage comes to life.   
  
More info on ajyal@usek.edu.lb

##  Bachelor of Arts in Performing Arts  (Open for Admission)
Multilingual 
126 credits
**_For students entering the program at the Freshman level_**  
(Please click here for more info on the [Freshman program](https://www.usek.edu.lb/academics/faculty-of-arts-and-sciences/academic-programs/freshman/freshman-arts?t=6))
96 credits
**_For students entering the program at the Sophomore level_**  
(holders of a recognized Baccalaureate or Freshman diploma - equivalent to 30 credits)  

## Courses
[ General Education](javascript:;)
[THT280Introduction to Acting](javascript:;)
3 credits
Introduction to different fundamental techniques used in the creation of a character. Emphasis on relaxation, concentration, and development of a role through sensorial and emotional memories. Students will improvise and do monologues as exercises in this introductory course. 
[ Specialization](javascript:;)
[MUS250Introduction to Voice Mastering ](javascript:;)
2 credits
Development of voice and speech techniques for the stage, including those of relaxation, breathing, resonance, and development of speaking voice. Speech training uses text work to train students in standard Arabic speech. 
[MUSC 210Choral Singing I](javascript:;)
1 credits
[MUSC350History of the 18th Century Music](javascript:;)
2 credits
This course opens on the years that mark the death of Jean­Sébastien Bach, the decline of the baroque era, with the dawn of the classical musical style. It deals with the following subjects: French (from 1661 to 1764) music, music of the Germanic countries around Bach and Handel, English music in the 18th century, the birth and diffusion of classicism in Polish music, music in Spain, the music in Italy from the death of Carissimi to the end of the eighteenth century, classicism in Austria and the German­speaking countries, from the death of Telemann to the death of Beethoven, the formation of the classical style in Europe and the classical masters: Haydn and Mozart. 
[SDO200Preparatory Solfeggio/Dictation](javascript:;)
2 credits
[THT215History of Theater](javascript:;)
3 credits
Study of history of theater from early western culture, Greek, renaissance, bourgeois, romantic, up to modern and post-modern theater. Egyptian and Lebanese theater is covered in this course. 
[THT230Introduction to Mime](javascript:;)
2 credits
Development of the physical capacities of the facial and body muscles to meet the exigencies of the characterization of a role. Advanced physical training of individual actors to their maximum potential. 
[THT240Physical theatre](javascript:;)
1 credits
[THT250Body expression](javascript:;)
2 credits
This course introduces students to the discovery of the body’s unique language, through exercises designed to explore and free the total instrument. It covers the development of a flexible actor with range, expression, and physical confidence, encouraging the awakening of the imagination while exploring the worlds of ritual, animal, conceptual, and modern dance movements. 
[THT260Analysis and Critic of Performing Arts I](javascript:;)
1 credits
Since Aristotle’s Poetics, the theatrical aesthetic appears as an intense questioning of theater and its practices. The aim of this course is to introduce the main theories of aesthetics. The position of many movements and genres will be explored. 
[THT310Dramaturgy](javascript:;)
3 credits
Theoretical and practical aspects of the dramaturge’s work in contemporary theater. Introduction to the study of theory and practice of dramaturgy. 
[THT320Advanced Acting](javascript:;)
3 credits
Development of an internal technique, beginning with an auto-drama which is a dramatization of one’s personal history. Development of an external technique through comedy. Fusion of the internal by use of action and objective with the external. 
[THT350History of Theater Directing](javascript:;)
3 credits
Investigation of the work of theater directors from the history of the world’s theater, with special emphasis on the relationship to time in which the work was generated. 
[THT355Costume & set design workshop](javascript:;)
3 credits
Investigation of the design research process, period style, and character analysis leading to visual presentation of the design. Study of costume design for theatrical productions, ballet, opera, and musical theater. 
[THT360Creative Writing](javascript:;)
3 credits
Study and analysis of varied aspects of the playwright’s art. Various aspects are selected from topics such as comedy writing, writing for children’s theater, and adaptation from literature to stage. 
[THT365Analysis and Critic of Performing Arts II](javascript:;)
1 credits
Following course 1, this course continues in introducing the main artistic movements. The aim of this course is to give a more solid academic grounding on theories of art criticism, providing reflection on major issues concerning the creation and reception of artistic work. 
[THT400Modern Drama](javascript:;)
3 credits
[THT405Performance and Contemporary Art](javascript:;)
3 credits
[THT415Puppet and Theatre for Children](javascript:;)
3 credits
Creative development and realization of production related to theater for children. Exploration of different techniques in the craft of the production of children’s theater. 
[THT430Theater of Puppets](javascript:;)
3 credits
Techniques of the manipulation of puppets, puppet movements, voice and performance. Development of skills through exercises which relate to theater of puppets. 
[THT440Directing and Production Workshop](javascript:;)
3 credits
Development of directorial skills through the medium of written preparations and directing of scenes. Application of stage directing techniques in the production of a short play. Students will direct a one-act play. 
[THT450Lighting & Sound Workshop](javascript:;)
3 credits
Study of use of light and color to define space, effect of light on scenery and costumes, lighting for theaters, patterns and moving scenery. Study of use of sound and acoustics as they relate to performance environments, techniques associated with recording, effects and music tracks for theater sound design. 
[THT460Analysis and Critic of Performing Arts III](javascript:;)
1 credits
The aim of this course (level 3) is to deepen knowledge in art theories and the interrelation between different arts through an intense exploration of the evolution of art since modernism, postmodernism, and the introduction to arts of new technologies. Students will apply the techniques of analysis and criticism to complex artistic work of arts. 
[THT465Performing Arts Production](javascript:;)
3 credits
Students will demonstrate knowledge of the performing arts industry, including live performance genres, production processes, careers and work environments. They will work creatively within a team to prepare and execute a live performance. 
[THT470Final Project](javascript:;)
3 credits
Students must produce a short play, 30 minutes maximum. 
[TLV232Make-up for films](javascript:;)
2 credits
[ Electives](javascript:;)
[EMU405Psychology and Music](javascript:;)
3 credits
[FLM240History of American Cinema](javascript:;)
3 credits
This course is designed to give students an understanding of the history of American cinema from its beginning in 1895 to the present time. It will focus on the silent cinema of D.W. Griffith, the Burlesque film of C. Chaplin and B. Keaton, the genre films of the studio era, the war and post­war noir film, the new Hollywood cinema of the 1960s, the films of the Movie Brats of the 1970s, and the post­modern cinema of the 1980s and on. Special attention will be given to the evolution of the art of the motion picture, including elements of camera, lighting, sound, editing, production design, and narrative structure and the technological evolution of the motion picture, including aspects of inventions and innovations such as color, widescreen, quality sound, and electronic imagery. 
[FLM344Theory aesthetics of films](javascript:;)
3 credits
This course focuses on the various theoretical methodologies that have developed in film theory and esthetics and that have proven useful for the analysis of films and cinema, such as realism, genre and auteur, reflexivity, intertextuality, psychoanalysis, and feminism. 
[MUG305Music and Dance](javascript:;)
2 credits
Attendance and participation are of primary importance for this class. We will work with a wide variety of techniques and styles, learn correct body alignment in basic positions, develop a kinesthetic awareness of his/her own physical abilities, develop a sense of musicality and rhythm. We will learn dances from the following list: Waltz, Tango, Cha cha, Salsa, Cumbia, Merengue, Foxtrot, Country Line Dance, Rumba, Swing or Samba and other. 
[MUS455Advanced Voice Mastering](javascript:;)
2 credits
Advanced voice techniques, with increased demands on range, resonance, and breathing capacity extension. Articulation and phonetic alphabet is emphasized. Text work in poetry and prose. 
[MUSC215Choral Singing II](javascript:;)
1 credits
Choral singing closely following the course of history. Each year the students learn to interpret, in the context of Western choral singing of the Faculty, the corresponding repertory according to the current history course. 
[MUSC246Arab Music I](javascript:;)
3 credits
[MUSC450History of the 19th Century Music](javascript:;)
2 credits
This course explores the music of the Romantic era. 1 ­ Characteristics of Romantic music: themes of Romanticism, individuality of style, expressive subjects, nationalism and exoticism, the use of timbers to obtain a variety of sensations and atmospheres, the use of chromatic harmony, contrasts in nuances etc. 2. Vocal music, program music, the Romantic Symphony, the brief forms and developed forms. 3. Romantic composers: Beethoven, Schubert, Schumann, Chopin, Liszt, Mendelssohn, Berlioz, Tchaikovsky, Smetana, Dvorak, Brahms, Verdi, Puccini, Wagner, Mahler. 
[PHO235Introduction to Photography Story-telling](javascript:;)
3 credits
Students will acquire techniques and tools to produce still images with sound tracks. Students will apply these techniques on a visual and audio project. 
[PSY214Developmental Psychology](javascript:;)
3 credits | Pre-requisite: PSY201
The course has two segments given in two sequential phases: Childhood and Adolescence 1st segment: childhood allows students to become familiar with basic concepts and notions of childhood developmental psychology (stages, phases and developmental factors); understand the major theoretical approaches (maturational, behavioral, psychoanalytical, cognitive constructivism and psychosocial approaches); identify the main characteristics belonging to each developmental stage on the biological, intellectual, affective, sexual, social and moral level; 2nd segment: adolescence allows students to understand the adolescent phase in the developmental process, note each function belonging to this stage, pinpoint the process of self­consolidation, the construction of the identity, achieving maturity as well as choices and decision­making processes. 
[SDG201Solfeggio/Dictation I](javascript:;)
2 credits
1st course   
a­ Solfeggio parlati : Pozzoli: Primo corso du n°1 au n°31   
b­ Solfeggio cantati: ­ Pozzoli: Primo corso du n°1 au n°31.   
c­ Dictation : ­ Noël Gallon du n°1 au n°20. ­ melodic intervals : 5th, 4th, octave, 3rd Maj and min, 2nd Maj and min. 
[SDG202Solfeggio/Dictation II](javascript:;)
2 credits | Pre-requisite: SDG201
2nd course   
a­ Solfeggio parlati : ­ Pozzoli: Primo corso du n°32 au n°60.   
b­ Solfeggio cantati: Pozzoli: Primo corso du n°32 au n°60.   
c­ Dictation : ­ Noël Gallon du n°21 au n°40. ­ melodic intervals : Triton, 6th Maj and min, 7th Maj and min. 
#### Mission
The Bachelor of Performing Arts is designed to give the student a broad-based understanding of the theatrical arts. Through study in this degree program, the student will develop both cognitive and affective skills in acting, dramatic writing, directing, lighting design, scenic design, costume design, construction and criticism as well as other aspects of theatre performance and theatre production. 
#### Program Educational Objectives
1. Graduates will acquire specific knowledge about the history of theater and shows, theories and practices of the scene and become familiar with the news of contemporary performance and new forms of expression in this field.  
2. Develop the acuity of judgment both in terms of creation and in the receiving plan.  
3. Acquire multiple stage technical performance.  
4. Learn to implement all the means to produce a complex spectacle, whether of body or voice, text (create, write or adaptation), or representation (choice of scenic place, creation a set design, implementation of sound, light or insertion of photographic or cinematographic images). 
#### Student Learning Outcomes
a. Students will be familiar with the types of spectacles and literary and scenic components. They will have to distinguish a spectacular kind of a subgenre, and to recognize the aesthetic trend to which it relates.  
b. Analyze methodically both a literary (read) and scenic dramatic work (presented on stage), identify scenic choice of directors, and to critically study on a show.  
c. Perform in shows of various kinds (theatrical play, play on camera, puppet animation, mime show, clown show and dancing etc.).  
d. Design a show, draw up the specifications for its production, plan rehearsals, recognize the difficulties it may be facing, identify possible solutions to the problems of implementation, team work and finally to mount a single show.

[ General Education](javascript:;)
[MUS243History of Lebanese Music](javascript:;)
3 credits
This course is designed to:   
1 - Sensitize students to Lebanese folk music.   
2 - Raise the students’ awareness of the threat to Lebanese folk music as an endangered and uncollected heritage that is hardly recorded in a scientific way; This includes the disappearance of certain songs as the circumstances underlying their writing and their raison d’être are no more, and the passing away of the old guard and keepers of tradition.   
3 – Introduce the students to the diverse forms – the well-known and the lesser known ones – of Lebanese music.   
4 - Study the internal poetic and musical structure of each traditional singing form.

[MUG330Music Languages](javascript:;)
2 credits
The goal of this course is to give to the students a general idea about the evolution of musical language from its beginning to the twentieth century: the scale of harmonics; the cycle of fifths, consonance and attraction, tolerance, habituation, equalization, the formation of the scales, relative pitch and absolute pitch, the organization of the sounds in space and in time, the melodic order and the harmonic order, the chromatic scale; the irregular and altered scales; from ditonic scale to heptatonic scale; accuracy and the acoustic systems; the equal temperament. 
[MUG335Musical Acoustics](javascript:;)
2 credits
This course concentrates on: vibratory motion of typical musical sound sources, propagation of sound, wavelength, period and frequency, pressure and acoustic intensity, the acoustic impedance speed, etc; perceived pitch, loudness and timbre of a sound; the objectively measurable properties of a sound wave; explaining how sound is generated - transformed by the musical instruments and the human voice; defining the reverberation time of a hall, using a formula relating reverberation time to the volume of the hall and the absorption of its surfaces, and discussing the acoustical properties desirable in concert halls and opera houses; microphones, amplifiers, speakers and sound captation acoustic treatment and correction.

[MUSC320Music Critique and Aesthetic Judgment III](javascript:;)
1 credits
This course includes a guided reading and musical critique, taking in readings in the literature and the science of music. Each student will have to read a book (or chapters in a book) per semester and present the content to others. The criticism is about:   
- Various reports and interviews, mainly in the field of contemporary musical creation.   
- Conception, realization and animation of a series of programs devoted to classical, modern and contemporary music.   
- A roundtable around musical works by various composers.   
- A report on a festival and concerts presented as part of this festival.   
- Leaflet of a compact disc, published flyers or texts in concert programs.   
- Symposia concerning music and conferences contained therein. 
[MUSC340Musical Forms](javascript:;)
2 credits
The examination of the form is a fundamental element of any analysis, because the form depends on the various components of a work, namely melody, rhythm, instrumentation, dynamics, tonal course, elements of unity and contrast ratio, relationship between text and music if it is a voice composition and other components. To understand musical forms, is to discern the sound architecture. 
[MUSC350History of the 18th Century Music](javascript:;)
2 credits
This course opens on the years that mark the death of Jean­Sébastien Bach, the decline of the baroque era, with the dawn of the classical musical style. It deals with the following subjects: French (from 1661 to 1764) music, music of the Germanic countries around Bach and Handel, English music in the 18th century, the birth and diffusion of classicism in Polish music, music in Spain, the music in Italy from the death of Carissimi to the end of the eighteenth century, classicism in Austria and the German­speaking countries, from the death of Telemann to the death of Beethoven, the formation of the classical style in Europe and the classical masters: Haydn and Mozart.

[MUSC400Organology and instrumentation](javascript:;)
3 credits
This course studies different musical instruments from antiquity to the present day, including the history, classifications, mechanics, acoustics, development, manufacturing, the different families of instruments, and helps deepen the concept of instrumentation and know the specificity of each instrument, in terms of timbres, register, transposition, combination of timbers, transcription, etc. 
[MUSC420Choir Conducting I](javascript:;)
1 credits
This course aims to train musicians on vocals, choirs and choir conducting. It includes concepts about the human voice and its education, the choir and its training, the conductor of the choir (values, posture, technique, behavior, etc.), choral conducting (departure gesture, the fermata, the stop gestures, the syncopation and offbeat, repeat, etc.). This course includes exercises on the evolution of the musical ear, on conductor gestures, on the conducting of simple meters (2/4, 3/4, 4/4).

[MUC201Chamber Music I](javascript:;)
1 credits
The aim of this music performance course is to provide the opportunity for the students as performers to come together with other like­minded musicians in an ensemble setting to rehearse and perform from the chamber orchestra repertoire. In this course we will focus on overall concepts of self and ensemble expression, engagement, participation, and performance. We will also address musical concepts of ensemble and individual balance, blend, intonation, phrasing, dynamics, articulation, tone, rhythmic precision, color, and ensemble clarity. We are going to listen to ourselves, to each other and to the composer’s voice.

2 credits
In music, transposition refers to the process, or operation, of moving a collection of notes (pitches or pitch classes) up or down in pitch by a constant interval.The circumstances that could lead a musician to transpose, either at sight or by rewriting the score, are diverse. One of the most common is the accompaniment to a singer whose tessitura is unsuited to the original key. Musicians playing a transposing instrument (clarinet, Horn, trumpet...) can be also brought to this practice, when they play a part that was not originally written for their instrument. The transposition at sight is to decrypt and transpose the score at the same time. It is a challenge requiring conversion training, more cerebral than spontaneous. Several methods are possible, but the most widely recognized, is the "transposition by the keys”, which consists of replacing the key used in the score – G clef, for example - by another key which gives the note corresponding to the transposition. At the same time, we need to change the armor and in some cases, accidentals - sharps, flats, etc. - indicated punctually on the score, using mathematical logic.

Several methods are possible, but the most widely recognized, is the "transposition by the keys”, which consists of replacing the key used in the score – G clef, for example - by another key which gives the note corresponding to the transposition. At the same time, we need to change the armor and in some cases, accidentals - sharps, flats, etc. - indicated punctually on the score, using mathematical logic. 
#### Emphasis
- Music Composition (Open for Admission)  
- Musical Instrument (Open for Admission)  
- Singing (Arabic Singing / Occidental Classical Singing) (Currently Not Open for Admission)  
- Solfeggio/Dictation (Open for Admission) 
#### Mission
The Department of Higher Specialized Music Education at USEK is committed to preparing, inspire and motivating students for excellence in professional careers in performance, composition and training.  
The Department provides a unique music culture and fosters the highest standards of teaching and supports the establishment of creative engagement through its own accomplishments, the work of its department members and staff and the achievement of its graduates.  
The Department strives to meet the educational needs of its diverse students through instruction, performance, scholarship, and public service; and generates creative music activities that have local, national and international significance. 
#### Program Educational Objectives
1. Graduates will meet standards of musical performance (through applied music studies, ensembles and master classes).  
2. Graduates will demonstrate competence in content­based areas of music history and analysis, advanced theory and musicianship, and music technology.  
3. Graduates will demonstrate competence in skill­based areas of ear training, sight singing, improvisation, composition and conducting.  
4. Graduates will demonstrate a working knowledge (an appropriate level of technical and interpretative performance skills), repertory in their major and performing skills - completely and expressively and providing leadership as a soloist, and as a member of performing ensembles.  
5. Graduates will demonstrate the ability to apply creative approaches to problem­solving and self­directed study, to conceive and realize musical programs and events. 
#### Student Learning Outcomes
a. Student will develop skills and understanding of music language and composition in a variety of styles, periods, and genres in both Western European tradition and Non­Western cultures.  
b. Develop skills of criticism and defend musical judgment, with reference to contextual meaning and aesthetic value in their own work, and the work of others.  
c. Develop a comprehensive knowledge and understanding of Western musical history and its analysis, and for the Arab and Lebanese music traditions.  
d. Develop technical skills and musical awareness for performance and leadership of both small and large choirs.  
e. Develop knowledge and skills in the use of technology, as it applies to notating, arranging, recording, and composing music.  
f. Develop a comprehensive knowledge and understanding of musical instruments, their classification systems, and the technical aspects related to their constructions and sound qualities and their use and importance in a composition.  
g. Develop knowledge and understanding of a variety of music businesses and industry practices.  
h. Develop a working knowledge of music as it relates to and enhances the theater and religious experience.  
i. Develop an acute ability to hear, analyze, read, write, and harmonize music at a basic level.   
j. Acquire sufficient understanding of advanced music theory, musical forms, processes, and structures, and use this knowledge in compositional and performance contexts.   
k. Develop knowledge and skills on a major instrument or voice, and the ability to read at sight.   
l. Develop skills that prepare them for careers in musical performance and private teaching of performance, and advanced study and independent practice, including significant technical mastery to solve professional problems, and a coherent set of artistic/intellectual goals that are evident in their work.   
m. Acquire artistic and technical skills, collaborative competence, and knowledge of repertory requisite for artistic self-expression in his major performance area.   
n. Develop an acute ability to identify and work conceptually with the elements of music at an advanced level.   
o. Develop a background in music and musicianship that prepares them for a wide range of further educational and vocational activities that include solfeggio and dictation as a basic component.

##  International Students Scholarship Program 
At USEK, we believe that education knows no borders. The International Students Scholarship Program (ISSP) is designed to support brilliant international students who aspire to pursue their academic dreams at one of Lebanon's top universities. This program aims to attract diverse talents from around the world, contributing to a vibrant multicultural environment that enriches our campus community.   
  
[ YOUR JOURNEY STARTS NOW! ](https://www.usek.edu.lb/Content/Assets/20250624isspBrochure-125751.pdf) |  |  |  [ APPLY HERE ](https://apply.usek.edu.lb/login?redirect-to=/usek-international-applicants/new#login)  
---|---|---|---  
  

[Benefits of Our Program](javascript:;)
The ISSP offers you the chance to: 
  * access quality education in one of Lebanon's top universities.
  * expand your cultural and scientific knowledge through immersive experiences.
  * pursue your higher education at USEK without financial constraints.
  * explore the Middle East from a unique perspective, engaging with Lebanese students for a richer cultural exchange.
  * enhance your language skills, both within the classroom and in your daily interactions on campus.
  * benefit from our [Be-A-Buddy Program](https://www.usek.edu.lb/internationl/be-a-buddy-program), which connects you with Lebanese USEK students to help you smoothly navigate your journey.
  * showcase your athletic talents, with the opportunity to join our esteemed sports teams.


[Eligibility, Admission, and Selection Process](javascript:;)
### Eligibility
- Scholarships are available for specific programs to international students living outside Lebanon. Eligible applicants include students of Lebanese origin residing abroad; however, binational students residing in Lebanon are not eligible.  
- Eligible applicants include international students seeking to pursue either a Bachelor’s or Master’s degree. Applicants should not be currently enrolled at USEK.  
- Applicants should meet USEK requirements for Bachelor’s or Master’s programs.   
  
**Undergraduate applicants are required to submit:**
  * a copy of their passport.
  * a motivation letter.
  * the official equivalent of the Lebanese Baccalaureate from the Ministry of Education and Higher Education (MEHE), if available.
  * a proficiency test equivalent.
  * an official secondary school transcript for grades 10, 11, and 12, clearly indicating the official curriculum.
  * a high school diploma (national or international).
  * a recommendation letter from the high school principal, including class ranking.

  
  
Graduate applicants are required to submit: 
  * a copy of their passport.
  * a motivation letter.
  * the official equivalent of the Lebanese undergraduate degree from the MEHE, if available.
  * an updated CV (PDF format – Word documents are not advised).
  * two academic recommendation letters.
  * a certified copy of the high school diploma (national or international).
  * a certified copy of the undergraduate degree from a nationally recognized institution.
  * the original official undergraduate transcript, including total credits and GPA.

  
  
Applicants must demonstrate good academic standing, with a minimum GPA of 80/100 or equivalent for undergraduate applicants and 85/100 or equivalent for graduate applicants.  
  

### Admission Criteria
Undergraduate applicants who meet any of the conditions below are exempt from taking the on-campus USEK English Proficiency Test: 
  * Redesigned SAT I Evidence-Based Reading and Writing with a score of 550/800 or 16/24 on the Optional Essay
  * Institutional Paper-Based TOEFL PBT with a score of 550/670
  * Computer-Based TOEFL CBT with a score of 213/300
  * Internet-Based TOEFL IBT with a score of 80/120
  * Cambridge First Certificate in English (now B2 First) with a score of C
  * International English Language Testing System (IELTS) with a score of 6/9

  
  
Graduate applicants applying for the following programs will be required to take the USEK English Proficiency Test (on campus) or an equivalent recognized English Proficiency Test: 
  * Master of Arts in Education
  * Master of Arts in English Language and Literature
  * Master of Arts in Cinema and Television
  * Master of Science in Biochemistry
  * Master of Science in Biology
  * Master of Science in Neuroscience and Biotechnology
  * Master of Science in Nutrition
  * Master of Science in Actuarial and Financial Mathematics

  
  
Graduate applicants who meet any of the conditions below are exempt from taking the on-campus USEK English Proficiency Test: 
  * Applicants who have completed a Bachelor's degree (or higher) in a country where English is the official language and the primary language of instruction for their academic program was English.
  * English proficiency test score requirements are:  
- TOEFL iBT (Internet-Based Test) ≥ 80  
- TOEFL PBT (Paper-Based Test) ≥ 550  
- IELTS (International English Language Testing System) ≥ 6  
- Duolingo English Test ≥ 105
  * Applicants may be required to undergo additional examinations, including oral assessments, depending on the specific requirements of the program to which they are applying.  
French Proficiency Test Requirements (only for programs that require French proficiency)
  * Applicants who meet any of the conditions below are exempted from taking the on-campus USEK French Proficiency Test:  
- DELF (B2) or TCF (B2)  
- An average of ≥ 10/20 in French (Grades 10 and 11)  
Undergraduate Program-Specific Test Requirements  
Below are the program-specific written test requirements:  
- Architecture Programs  
Redesigned SAT I (Evidence-Based Reading and Writing + Math) ≥ 1200/1600, or the on-campus USEK Math Entrance Exam ≥ 70/100  
- Business Programs  
Redesigned SAT I (Evidence-Based Reading and Writing + Math) ≥ 1100/1600 or the on-campus USEK Math Entrance Exam ≥ 70/100  
- Humanities and Art Programs  
Redesigned SAT I (Evidence-Based Reading and Writing) ≥ 550/800 or Essay SAT ≥ 16/24  
- Sciences Programs  
- Redesigned SAT I (Evidence-Based Reading and Writing + Math) ≥ 1100/1600 or the on-campus USEK Math Entrance Exam ≥ 70/100.
  * Applicants who are enthusiastic about participating in USEK athletic activities are encouraged to apply. 

  
  

### APPLICATION
Interested students are invited to apply at APPLY - USEK - Login.  
Incomplete applications will not be considered.  
  

### SELECTION PROCESS
- Eligibility Check  
An initial review of all received applications will be conducted to ensure they meet the minimum eligibility criteria.  
  
- Verification of Documents  
The Scholarship Committee will verify that all required documents have been submitted. Undergraduate applicants are required to submit specific proficiency test results, while graduate applicants are required to submit proficiency test results for certain programs. These requirements are outlined under the “Eligibility” section above.  
  
- Academic Evaluation  
Applications will be evaluated based on academic performance.  
  
- Review of Extracurricular Activities  
The Committee will assess the applicants' involvement in extracurricular activities.  
  
- Review of Letters  
All applicants will be evaluated based on the content and quality of their motivation and recommendation letters.  
  
- Faculty Interview  
Online interviews or oral examinations with relevant heads of departments may be required. Applicants will be notified in advance regarding the scheduling of these assessments.  
  
- Diversity and Inclusion Consideration  
The Committee will strive to ensure diversity and inclusion in the final selection, considering factors such as nationality, background, and life experience.  
  
- Final Selection  
Based on the comprehensive evaluation, the Committee will make the final selection of scholarship recipients.  
  
- Notification  
All applicants will be informed of the Committee's decision regarding their application.  
  
- Completion of Declaration of Document Submission Form  
Applicants are required to sign a form whereby they pledge to provide the necessary equivalent documents, certified by the MEHE, within six months of their registration.  
  
_N.B. The Scholarship Committee will oversee the process to ensure it is transparent, fair, and free from discrimination._  
  

### What the Scholarship Covers
The scholarship covers full tuition fees for Bachelor's and Master's programs, excluding remedial courses. However, applicants are responsible for paying registration fees each semester, travel expenses to and from Lebanon, as well as housing and living costs.  
  
_N.B. Students may be required to complete remedial courses under specific circumstances and for certain programs._
[Conditions for Maintaining the Scholarship](javascript:;)
Continued eligibility for the scholarship in successive semesters is contingent upon maintaining a minimum GPA throughout the course of study. For Bachelor's programs, a minimum GPA of 80/100 is required, while for Master's programs, the minimum GPA is 85/100.  
  
The USEK International Students’ Scholarship will be forfeited in any of the following instances: 
  * Academic probation.
  * Change of academic program.
  * Interruption of studies.
  * Term withdrawal (WW)
  * Part‐time enrollment (less than 12 credits per semester for undergraduate studies or less than 6 credits per semester for graduate studies).
  * Upon the decision of the Disciplinary Council in the event of a breach of the Code of Conduct.
  * Enrollment in an exchange program.

_Applications are not accepted for Spring Semesters or Summer Sessions._
